title: Manage hive placement and bee pollination

lessons.title: Pollination services and hive placement
lessons.html:
Why crops need bees

Many South African crops depend heavily on insect pollination, especially by honeybees: apples, pears, plums and cherries in the Western Cape, macadamias and avocados in Limpopo and Mpumalanga, blueberries, canola, sunflower seed production, cucurbits and many seed crops. Poor pollination shows as low fruit set, misshapen fruit and lower yields. Most commercial pollination uses hives of the Cape or African honeybee hired from a beekeeper for the flowering period.

Planning a pollination contract

  • Agree the number of hives, the strength of each colony (for example number of frames covered with bees and brood), delivery and removal dates, and price per hive in ZAR.
  • Hives should arrive when a small percentage of flowers are open, not weeks before, or bees may find other forage first.
  • Agree in writing which pesticides may be used during flowering and how the beekeeper will be warned.

Placing hives

  • Spread hives in groups through the orchard or field rather than all at the edge, because bees work most intensively near the hive.
  • Choose sites with access for the beekeeper's vehicle at night, away from footpaths, houses, kraals and stables.
  • Face entrances towards morning sun if possible, on stands that keep them off damp ground and away from ants.
  • Provide clean water close by; bees need it to cool the hive.
  • Remove competing flowering weeds under trees where practical, so bees focus on the crop.

Hive stocking rates vary with crop, variety and colony strength; get recommendations from the crop industry body or an experienced pollination beekeeper.

lessons.title: Protecting bees and people
lessons.html:
Pesticides and bees

Pesticide poisoning is a major cause of colony losses. During flowering, the grower and beekeeper share responsibility for protecting bees.

  • Read the label: many insecticides are marked as toxic to bees and must not be applied to crops in flower or when bees are foraging.
  • If a spray is unavoidable, choose a product safer for bees, spray late in the evening when bees are not flying, and notify the beekeeper in advance so hives can be closed or moved.
  • Prevent drift onto hives, water sources and flowering weeds.
  • Never rinse spray equipment where bees drink.

Safety around bees

African honeybees can be very defensive. Workers near hives must know the risks.

  • Keep tractors, mowers and loud machinery away from hive groups, or work there only when the beekeeper agrees.
  • Only trained people in a bee suit, veil and gloves, using a smoker, should open hives.
  • If attacked, protect your face, move quickly away to a building or vehicle and do not swat or jump into water.
  • Remove stings by scraping with a fingernail or card.
  • Anyone with a known bee allergy must carry their prescribed medication and tell the supervisor. Signs of a severe allergic reaction (swelling of face or throat, difficulty breathing, collapse) are an emergency: call for medical help immediately. First aid training by an accredited provider is required for responders.

Evaluating pollination

Check bee activity on flowers on warm mornings, compare fruit set between blocks and keep records of hive numbers and yields each season. Use these to adjust hive numbers and placement next year.

Key points

  • Bring hives in at the start of flowering, with agreed colony strength.
  • Distribute hives through the crop with water nearby.
  • Never spray bee-toxic products on flowering crops while bees forage.
  • Communicate spray plans to the beekeeper.
  • Keep people and machinery away from hives; treat severe stings as an emergency.
